## Editorial policy
# Agentic GRC: Editorial Policy (version 2)

Owner: Iva Biscanic. This policy is supplied to the AI at every editorial stage
(selection, briefs, articles, video scripts). The AI applies it; I review its decisions.

## 1. Audience and purpose
Readers are executives and risk, compliance and security leaders (CEO, COO, CFO, CISO),
consultants and researchers working with critical-infrastructure operators in Europe and the
US. They understand AI and their sector's regulation. They lack a clear view of where current
frameworks fall short for **agentic AI**: systems that plan and act with some autonomy.
Central question: *As AI agents start acting autonomously in critical infrastructure, which
risks are real, which claims are hype, and what do current governance frameworks require
operators to do?*

## 2. Relevance (what we cover)
Accept material that bears directly on at least one of:
- **R1 AI agents in critical-infrastructure operations**: energy, grids, telecom, water,
  transport, OT/ICS; deployment, oversight, failures, controls, vendor access.
- **R2 Rules and frameworks**: EU AI Act, NIS2, Cyber Resilience Act, NIST AI RMF, NIST CSF,
  FERC/NERC CIP, sector regulators, standards (e.g. ISO/IEC 42001), procurement rules.
- **R3 AI data centres as critical infrastructure**: grid connection, reliability standards,
  energy demand, security, local opposition, and what this means for operators.
- **R4 Governance precedents** (not about AI itself): how a regulator turns an emerging-technology
  risk into concrete requirements for critical-infrastructure operators (exposure assessment,
  migration plans, deadlines, verifiable readiness criteria), e.g. quantum-safe migration mandates.
  **Guardrail:** R4 evidence may support only an analogy or inference about AI, labelled as such;
  it must never be the only evidence for a claim about AI systems.
An item counts as R1-R3 only if its text explicitly discusses AI, machine learning or autonomous
agents. General OT or critical-infrastructure security content without AI is R4 or rejected.
AI-enabled attacks on infrastructure are relevant **only** when the item changes what
operators must do to govern their own AI systems; otherwise reject.
Reject: general geopolitics, defence and military dependencies, macro-economic or industrial-policy
debates, consumer AI, product promotions, and AI news with no link to critical infrastructure or
governance. If an item fits none of R1-R4, reject it; do not stretch a category to fit.

## 3. Freshness and novelty
- Only material published within the 30-day window is used (enforced mechanically before
  selection). Publication date and collection date are kept separate.
- **Republished material** (e.g. "Archive" episodes, reposted recordings, refreshed dates on
  old articles) is **deferred** unless it contains something newly reported; the reason must
  say what is old and what, if anything, is new. Titles containing "Archive", "Rewind", "Encore"
  or "Rebroadcast", or an introduction saying the recording is from an earlier date, signal
  republication even when the feed date is new.
- When a recent source discusses an older event, say so and state what is newly learned.
- Several outlets repeating the same announcement count as **one underlying claim**, not
  independent corroboration.

## 4. Credibility (judged per claim, not per source)
- Reputation, popularity or the model's own confidence are never enough on their own.
- Prefer primary evidence: regulator documents, audit findings, incident data, named
  practitioners describing their own experience, published methods.
- **Vendor and commercial content** (e.g. Dragos, IBM, AWS, consultancies) is usable but is a
  `source_claim`: note the commercial incentive and look for independent corroboration.
  A vendor presenting or demonstrating its own platform, product series or service is
  **promotional and rejected**, even when the tone is educational, unless it reports specific,
  checkable results about AI in operations (what was deployed, where, with what outcome or failure).
- Think-tank and podcast opinion is interpretation; label it as such.
- Unsupported claims (no data, no method, no named source) are not used as facts.

## 5. Uncertainty and conflicting evidence
- Distinguish `reported_fact`, `source_claim` and `inference` (my interpretation).
- When sources conflict, present both, explain why they may differ (scope, incentives, data),
  and say what would settle it. Do not invent disagreement where the evidence agrees.
- State remaining uncertainty explicitly. If the evidence does not justify a conclusion,
  say so rather than forcing one.

## 6. Diversity of perspectives
Each piece should draw on at least three independent publishers and, across the series,
on policy/research, industry/vendor and practitioner perspectives, using written, video and
podcast evidence. Known gaps to state openly: operators' own voices, EU regulators and
agencies (e.g. ENISA), workers and affected communities, non-US/EU perspectives.

## 7. Geography
EU and US weighted equally. Prefer evidence that allows a transatlantic comparison.

## 8. Voice
Plain, precise, non-alarmist English for senior professionals. Short paragraphs, no hype
words, no marketing tone. Every substantive claim is traceable to evidence.

## 9. Exclusions
No undated material as evidence. No invented sources, quotes or numbers. No personal data
about private individuals. AI-generated presentation is disclosed.

## Change log
- **v2 (2026-10-18)**, after reviewing live run 1 (docs/review_run1.md). The model accepted a vendor
  platform walkthrough with no AI content that v1 already excluded (after rejecting it in an earlier call),
  and stretched R3 to fit a non-AI regulatory item. Changes: stricter vendor rule (own-platform
  walkthroughs are promotional); R1-R3 require explicit AI content; new R4 for governance precedents
  with a guardrail; "do not stretch a category" rule; concrete republication signals; military
  dependencies and industrial-policy debates added to the reject list.
- **v1 (2026-10-18)**: initial policy.


## The three planned pieces
- 01: What changed, and which developments matter most to this audience?
- 02: Which claims withstand scrutiny, and where are the evidence or interpretations in tension?
- 03: What do these developments imply for the audience, and what should they watch next?

## Task
For EVERY item below, decide:
- "accept": relevant under policy section 2, credible enough to use, and useful for at least
  one piece. Give the piece_ids it would serve.
- "reject": off-topic, promotional without substance, or unusable. piece_ids must be [].
- "defer": possibly relevant but republished/old, duplicative of another item, or too thin to
  use now. piece_ids must be [].
The reason must cite the policy section(s) applied (e.g. "R1; 4 vendor claim") and be specific
to this item: what it contributes, or why it fails. Do not judge credibility by reputation alone.
Also give "credibility_note" (what kind of evidence it offers and any commercial incentive) and
"relevance" (R1, R2, R3 or none).

RIYADH—Even as Houthi missiles rain down on Saudi Arabia, there is an eerie calm in Riyadh. King Fahd Road, the capital’s main artery, is jammed with traffic. Chic women sip Japanese matcha in French cafes, designer American labels peeking out from under their abayas. At a glance, Riyadh feels like business as usual: a buzzing metropolitan coming into its own. An outsider might never guess that the airport is closed for the foreseeable future, that schools and many offices have gone remote, or that we were awakened last night by text alarms and the boom-boom-boom of intercepts. In just three days, Riyadh’s international airport was attacked not once but three times, leaving at least twelve people dead and more than three hundred injured. This, despite a growing network of security partners and commitments to military assistance. But Saudis have waited decades for the new Saudi Arabia. They will not let it go quietly. New friends, same problems Saudis have spent the past decade working to diversify not only their economy, but also their diplomatic and security relationships. As relations with the United States have fluctuated and their Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) neighbors increasingly shifted from partnership to rivalry, Riyadh has turned elsewhere. The Saudis have made notable diplomatic overtures to China and Russia and sought renewed defense agreements with the French, Italians, and British, all to supplement US support. More recently, Saudi Arabia entered into the highly publicized Mecca Agreement with Pakistan and Turkey. Signed in August, the NATO-lite pact declares that an attack on one is an attack on all. It was meant to strengthen deterrence and signal strategic realignment. Just two months later, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have put the agreement to its first real test. So far, however, the impact has been lackluster. Pakistan had already deployed roughly eight thousand troops, a squadron of fighter jets, drones, and a Chinese-made air-defense system to Saudi Arabia months before the agreement was signed. The day after the attacks, Islamabad promised to deploy additional forces, but has not specified how many and so far has publicly ruled out a deployment to Yemen. Turkey, for its part, is supplying Saudi Arabia with air defense equipment, intelligence, drones, and other technical assistance, but its parliament has yet to ratify the agreement. Despite strong statements of solidarity, neither country is willing to commit to a broader military campaign in Yemen it remains unclear how far their contributions have been integrated into Saudi Arabia’s broader air-defense architecture. US support, meanwhile, runs wide and deep, and US officials are quick to remind you of that. Washington provides weapons, training, technical support, and intelligence that are indispensable—indeed, irreplaceable. US-supplied Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) systems are central to Saudi missile defense. In the past two years, Washington has been piling on support. A series of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centers have made international headlines this week amid speculation that Ukraine’s attacks succeeded in temporarily silencing the bot networks driving Moscow’s global disinformation operations. While multiple industry experts have subsequently questioned these claims, there is no doubt that Kyiv’s bombing offensive has demonstrated the vulnerability of Russia’s heavily concentrated digital infrastructure. In early October, Ukrainian long-range drones struck three of the five main data centers belonging to Yandex, a tech giant that is often referred to as “Russia’s Google.” All three of these mega data centers sustained significant damage. Social media users around the world were soon reporting a sharp decline in bot activity, with many attributing this to Ukraine’s drone strike campaign. Addressing the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy commented on this trend. “When our strikes reached Yandex data centers, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms,” the Ukrainian leader commented. “A lot of people noticed it. There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots. And it’s pretty clear where those bots were coming from.” Not everyone is convinced. While large numbers of social media users reported fewer bots and declining engagement for Kremlin-friendly accounts, others have been more skeptical regarding the impact of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s online influence activities. “We can’t simply bomb the bots out of existence, however appealing that might sound,” Ned Mendez of Alliance4Europe told Britain’s Guardian newspaper. “They aren’t really a single set of buildings that can be switched off.” Stay updated As the world watches the Russian invasion of Ukraine unfold, UkraineAlert delivers the best Atlantic Council expert insight and analysis on Ukraine twice a week directly to your inbox. Opinion remains divided over the impact of Ukraine’s airstrikes on Russia bot activity, but the wider damage caused by the attacks is not in doubt. Over the past week, many of the digital services provided by Yandex and partner companies have been disrupted or forced offline by the Ukrainian bombing campaign. On October 11, Russian customers of Yandex online banking services were unable to access the app or reach their funds. “I understand that you are waiting not for words but for access to your money,” commented Yandex financial services head Dmitry Pirogov in a social media post that gave no date for a full recovery. A wide range of Yandex apps and tools including taxi services encountered similar difficulties. The disruption went far beyond Yandex’s own platforms. More than sixty thousand Russian businesses and institutions rely on the company’s online services, including everything from fast food delivery and smart home management to e-commerce and municipal administrations. Many reportedly experienced difficulties in the wake of Ukraine’s drone strikes. title: Iraq’s militias are adjusting for a new era, not going away
published_at: 2026-10-16T14:58:34Z
url: https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/menasource/iraqs-militias-are-adjusting-for-a-new-era-not-going-away/
excerpt:
Iran-backed militias in Iraq are celebrating their “victory” over the United States following the completion of the withdrawal of US forces from Iraq. They are adjusting their posture for a new era in Iraq, signaling restraint, and continuing to pursue the completion of their state capture project. This “restraint” is designed to facilitate deeper entrenchment by easing US pressure on Baghdad while preserving the militias’ military capabilities. A statement by Kataib Hezbollah Secretary General Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi illustrates this posture. He ordered his fighters to halt “all military operations and mobile logistical activities,” but explicitly retained an exception for targeting hostile aircraft violating Iraqi airspace until government air defenses are fully established. The withdrawal of US forces leaves fewer targets inside Iraq, making the announced halt relatively low-cost. Washington has threatened to impose sanctions on Iraqi oil revenues unless Baghdad works to curb the influence of the militias, and announcing a halt gives the government an argument against taking forceful measures. The militias have little incentive to invite financial restrictions that would deepen Iraq’s already severe economic problems and damage their own sources of funding and patronage. Tehran shares this interest in protecting Iraq’s economic viability. Under mounting sanctions, Iran increasingly depends on Iraq as an outlet through which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Quds Force and its proxies can access hard currency and evade sanctions, giving both the militias and their Iranian patrons a reason to support the tactical pause. A Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) bill provides a further incentive for this tactical restraint. On September 29, the cabinet approved and referred to parliament an eighteen-article organizational bill governing the PMF’s structure and leadership. Although the PMF already has legal recognition and state funding, the new measure would be dedicated legislation, strengthening its position as a separate military institution and increasing its claim on the national budget. For the militias within it, this could mean stronger legal protections, greater funding, and access to military infrastructure without effective state control. Halting attacks could help ease US scrutiny and the threat of sanctions, facilitating the PMF’s consolidation as a parallel army. Al-Hamidawi explicitly advocated for this arrangement in a recent statement, calling for the “resistance” to remain a military force alongside the government’s armed forces. He described this as “a virtue and a good thing” and argued that many countries have more than one army or military organization. Yet the militias within this parallel army show little sign of behaving as responsible, professional forces accountable to Baghdad. Instead, they increasingly act as proxies at the IRGC’s disposal. During the first months of the US–Israeli war against Iran, much of the PMF’s state-funded personnel, bases, and logistical infrastructure mobilized in support of Tehran’s war effort. Thirty-six PMF brigades—roughly half the force—were implicated in conducting attacks or providing material support to the groups carrying them out. excerpt:
Measuring Europe’s rearmament: A year of the Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030 Bottom lines up front - It has been one year since the EU released the Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030, a detailed plan to measure and close Europe’s capability gaps. - Fifteen of the roadmap’s milestones are on track or complete; seventeen are not; the status of thirteen milestones is unclear. - Instead of trying to entirely replace the US, Europe should focus on the key capabilities it can’t currently produce and that the US has suggested it will pull back. Table of contents Introduction European security is increasingly a European Union issue. The security role the bloc plays today would have been unimaginable just a decade ago. Immediate concerns over the threat Russia poses to Europe and increasing uncertainty about Washington’s commitment to Europe have pushed European Member states to let the EU take unprecedented action in the security and defense space. The launch of the Pentagon’s Europe Force Posture Review on July 29 is only the latest reminder that the United States’ posture on the continent remains in flux. Member states are still in the driver’s seat on security matters, but the EU has found ways to play a role, particularly to help pool resources to better address threats together and support collaborative and flagship European defense projects. Previous strategies, such as the White Paper on European Defence, the SAFE lending mechanism, and the ReArm Europe Plan/Readiness 2030 each sought to boost public and private investment in defense and give Member States greater financial flexibility to strengthen production and readiness. An immediate critique that can be raised to the EU’s many such plans and strategies, however, is the lack of follow-through. The EU excels at grand outlines but struggles with the tactical steps to achieve its ambitions. It is for this reason that the EU’s detailed Defence Readiness Roadmap 2030 stands out. Published in October 2025, the document serves as a yardstick, providing measurable goals, concrete benchmarks, and specific deliverables to the various ideas such as those previously sketched out in the White Paper, for example. The roadmap pays special focus to four flagship projects and nine capability indicators against which Europe’s progress towards full defense readiness can be tracked. A year on, the EU has currently completed or is on track to complete fifteen of the roadmap’s stated milestones, but it has missed or is not on track to meet seventeen. The status of the remaining thirteen is unclear. While the roadmap clearly lays out the capabilities Europe needs to develop in the future, it is important that a smaller number of critical gaps are prioritized now to effectively manage limited resources and ensure Europe’s ongoing security in both the near term and the long term. This report will assess the EU’s progress towards the goals it set for itself in the roadmap and suggest a way forward to ensure the defense readiness of the Union. title: What Ukraine’s Starlink disruptions reveal about the tradeoffs involved in military commercial dependencies
published_at: 2026-10-16T22:17:34Z
url: https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatches/what-ukraines-starlink-disruptions-reveal-about-the-tradeoffs-involved-in-military-commercial-dependencies/
excerpt:
WASHINGTON—Earlier this week, Ukrainian forces reportedly were forced to cancel drone missions amid sudden restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, that interrupted their communications. Ukrainian officials and military units reported dropped connections and lowered operation speeds, although the full extent of the disruptions and the reasons behind them remain unclear. By October 15, connectivity had been restored. But the incident exposed a vulnerability with implications beyond Ukraine. Over the past several years, Ukraine has demonstrated how commercially available technology can be rapidly adapted for military purposes, often providing capabilities that would otherwise take years to develop and field. Indeed, there are certainly lessons to be learned from Ukraine’s success in rapidly getting new capabilities into the hands of warfighters. But the reported Starlink disruptions also illustrate a risk that deserves greater attention as the United States itself moves toward greater reliance on commercial technology or infrastructure: What happens when a military becomes dependent on capabilities it does not own, operate, or ultimately control? 1. What do Ukraine’s Starlink disruptions tell us about the risks of military dependence on commercial infrastructure? It is important to distinguish between two related SpaceX technologies: Starlink and Starshield. Starlink is a commercial satellite internet service that uses a constellation of satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity through relatively small, portable ground terminals. Unlike terrestrial communications infrastructure, Starlink can provide service in areas where conventional networks have been damaged, destroyed, or are unavailable. This capability has made it particularly valuable to Ukrainian forces, whose communications infrastructure has faced persistent threats from Russian strikes and electronic warfare. Starshield, by contrast, is SpaceX’s defense-oriented offering, designed specifically for government and national security customers. While it draws on technologies developed for Starlink, Starshield incorporates additional security and mission-specific capabilities to support military communications, intelligence collection, and other national security operations. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Starlink and Starshield have become an important part of Ukraine’s military communications network, supporting command and control, situational awareness, intelligence sharing, and drone operations. To be clear, neither Starlink nor Starshield independently makes military decisions. Their communications capabilities, however, help connect sensors, commanders, and operational units, enabling the information sharing needed for threat detection and operational coordination. Recognizing the importance of satellite communications to Ukraine’s military, the Pentagon contracted with SpaceX to provide Starlink services. According to Ukrainian military officials, the restrictions imposed on October 14 primarily affected military-grade Starshield services, particularly terminals operating aboard drones traveling at higher speeds. The restrictions reported interrupted connections and canceled missions, although there is no indication that Ukraine’s entire Starlink network was disabled. While connectivity appears to be back, questions remain about what caused the disruption and what its operational impact was. It would be easy to see this as a connectivity problem, but the implications run much deeper. title: Russia’s Starlink substitute poses a security threat far beyond Ukraine
published_at: 2026-10-15T19:53:34Z
url: https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/ukrainealert/russias-starlink-substitute-poses-a-security-threat-far-beyond-ukraine/
excerpt:
The Russian invasion of Ukraine has underlined the role of space communications infrastructure in securing internet connectivity on the modern battlefield. Russia is currently developing a satellite network project meant to serve as a domestic alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink. This could give the Kremlin a dangerous edge in Ukraine, while transforming the security and space safety landscape on a global scale. Since it was established in 2015, SpaceX owned low-earth orbit (LEO) constellation Starlink has been the major driver in the development of global satellite connectivity. Following the onset of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Starlink has provided vital support for Ukraine as the Russian military has repeatedly attacked every part of the country’s communications infrastructure. Satellites are exceptionally difficult to disrupt, while constant connectivity on the battlefield is an invaluable resource. Starlink has also highlighted the need for countries to have reliable connectivity. On October 13, restrictions were suddenly and without any prior announcement introduced to Starlink in Ukraine, disrupting military operations. The Kremlin is now in the process of deploying its own satellite network, known as Rassvet.
